name: Tongue stretching exercises
lead: Tongue stretching exercises are exercises in which the tongue is extended or held in a stretched position, either by the person alone or with assistance. In looksmaxxing and voice-related discussion they are sometimes said to lower the voice, although that purpose is not what the exercises have been studied for.

In the published literature, tongue stretching exercises appear in swallowing (dysphagia) rehabilitation. A small 2019 randomized controlled trial in 25 stroke patients with dysphagia tested a four-week program of dynamic and static passive tongue stretching delivered by an occupational therapist, and examined tongue motility and oromotor function.[1] No published study located for this article has tested whether tongue stretching changes voice pitch in healthy people.

paras: The exercises involve protruding, lifting or stretching the tongue, sometimes with manual assistance, to increase its range of movement. The studied clinical version divides them into dynamic and static passive stretching performed with a therapist.[1]

One preliminary double-blind randomized controlled trial (2019) assigned 25 post-stroke patients with dysphagia to tongue stretching exercises (13) or a control group (12) for four weeks, with outcomes of tongue motility and oromotor function.[1] It was a small preliminary study in a patient population, and it did not measure voice pitch or appearance outcomes. No studies found on tongue stretching and voice pitch in healthy adults.

Reference sources give typical adult speaking fundamental frequencies of roughly 90 to 155 Hz for men and 165 to 255 Hz for women.[2] Voice therapy as described by speech-language pathologists works on parameters such as vocal fold closure, pitch, volume and quality, and includes exercises like gliding between low and high pitches; its descriptions do not list tongue stretching as a pitch-lowering technique.[3]

refs.title: Tongue stretching exercises improve tongue motility and oromotor function in patients with dysphagia after stroke: A preliminary randomized controlled trial

card.summary: Tongue stretches said to deepen the voice; the only trial is in stroke swallowing rehab, not voice.
card.note: Studied only for swallowing after stroke; no voice-pitch data.

quick.overview:
Tongue stretching exercises involve extending or stretching the tongue. Some voice-focused circles say they lower the voice.

The only trial located tested them in 25 stroke patients with swallowing difficulty, looking at tongue movement rather than voice.
quick.mechanism: In the clinical setting, a therapist stretches the tongue passively to improve its mobility. No mechanism linking this to lower vocal pitch has been tested.
quick.risks: No adverse effects were described in the available abstract, and no safety data exist for the voice-related use. No published study supports or refutes an effect on voice pitch.
